opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to see it is that post-training has become a pipeline of stages, and RL is increasingly where a lot of the most interesting capability gains happen.

The classic picture was pretraining gives you a huge base model with broad knowledge, then supervised fine-tuning teaches it the format: how to be an assistant, follow instructions, respond in a chat. Then RL, originally RLHF, did the final polish: aligning outputs with human preferences, making the model more helpful, less likely to say weird things. In that framing, RL was a small finishing touch.

What's changed over the last couple of years is that RL is no longer just polish. Once you have verifiable rewards, like math problems with checkable answers, code that passes or fails tests, or tasks in an environment where you can tell whether the agent succeeded, RL becomes a way to teach skills, not just style. The model generates attempts, you score them, and it learns from its own successes. That's how you get long chains of reasoning, self-correction, and the ability to work through multi-step problems that are hard to demonstrate with supervised data alone. You can't easily write down the ideal thought process for every hard problem, but you can check whether the answer is right.

So the way I'd frame it now: SFT gets the model into the right region, teaching it formats and behaviors and giving it a decent prior. RL then lets the model explore within that region and sharpen behaviors that actually lead to good outcomes. They're complementary. RL works much better when the starting policy is already reasonable, because if the model never stumbles onto a correct answer, there's no signal to learn from.

For deployment specifically, I think RL matters more and more as we move toward agents. If you want a model that uses tools, navigates a codebase, or operates over many turns, the behaviors you care about are about outcomes over long horizons. That's a natural fit for RL, and a lot of the work going forward is about building good environments and good reward signals, figuring out what "success" means for a task in a way that's robust and doesn't get hacked.

The flip side is that RL is finicky. Reward hacking is real, models find shortcuts, and you need careful evaluation to make sure you're improving the thing you care about and not just the metric. But overall, I'd say RL has gone from the cherry on top to one of the core engines of post-training, especially for reasoning and agentic capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL’s growing role and capabilities but does not say it consumes most post-training compute.

r002.rationale: It presents RL as one stage in a broader post-training pipeline and discusses its role in preparing models for deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that RL is really the last mile of post-training, but it's a last mile that's become a lot more important than it used to be. If you go back a couple years, the pipeline was basically pretraining, then supervised fine-tuning on a bunch of human-written demonstrations, and then some kind of RLHF on top to shape the style and make the model more helpful and less likely to say things you don't want it to say. And in that world, RL was kind of a polish step. It made the model nicer to interact with, but it wasn't really where the capability was coming from.

What's changed is that people figured out you can use RL to actually make models better at things, not just more agreeable. If you have a task where you can check whether the model got it right, whether that's math, or code that has to pass tests, or an agent that has to actually accomplish something in an environment, then you can let the model try a bunch of times, reward the attempts that work, and the model genuinely learns to do the thing. It learns to reason longer, to verify its own work, to recover from mistakes. That's not polish anymore. That's capability.

So the way I think about the broader process now is that pretraining gives you the raw material, the knowledge and the latent ability. SFT is sort of the on-ramp, it gets the model into the right format and the right basin so RL has something to work with. And then RL is where you actually shape behavior toward outcomes that matter for deployment. And "outcomes that matter" is the key phrase, because the thing RL is really good at is optimizing against whatever signal you give it. If your reward is well-aligned with what users actually want, that's great. If it's not, the model will find the gap and exploit it. So a huge amount of the work is really in designing environments and reward functions, more than in the algorithm itself.

The other thing I'd say is that this is pushing more of the work out of the frontier labs and toward anyone who has a real task. Because the bottleneck now is less about having some secret RL algorithm and more about having good environments that reflect the thing you actually care about. If you're deploying a model for customer support or for some specific coding workflow, the most valuable thing you can build is a faithful simulation of that task with a signal for whether the model did well. That's where I think a lot of the interesting work is going to be over the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL as an increasingly important “last mile,” but does not say it consumes most post-training compute.

r002.rationale: The response places RL alongside pretraining and supervised fine-tuning in the broader process of shaping a model for deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as one part of the post-training process, where you move from a model that can produce plausible responses to one that reliably does what you want. You might start with supervised fine-tuning to demonstrate the behavior you’re looking for, and then use reinforcement learning to let the model try different approaches and learn from feedback about which ones work better.

The central question is what feedback you can provide. For something like coding, you can run tests and get a fairly concrete signal. For a general assistant, helpfulness is harder to measure, and whatever reward you use will be an imperfect proxy. So improving that reward isn’t automatically the same as improving the deployed product.

That makes RL part of an iterative process: define the behavior you want, train against the best signals you have, and evaluate whether the gains actually carry over to realistic use. It can be a powerful way to refine a model’s behavior, but it doesn’t replace careful evaluation or the rest of the deployment work.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL as part of post-training but does not state that it consumes most of the post-training compute for large-scale models.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls reinforcement learning “one part of the post-training process” and says it does not replace the rest of deployment work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of reinforcement learning as one part of post-training, rather than the whole thing. You start with a pretrained model that has a broad range of capabilities, and then you’re trying to turn that into something that behaves reliably in a particular setting. Supervised fine-tuning gives it examples of what good behavior looks like. Reinforcement learning lets it generate responses, get feedback, and adjust toward the outcomes you care about.

The key question is what that feedback actually rewards. If you can check whether an answer is correct or whether a task was completed, you have a useful signal. If you’re relying on a preference model, you have to be careful that improving the score corresponds to improving the experience for the user.

So I’d put RL inside an iterative process: define the behavior you want, train toward it, evaluate where it fails, and improve the data or the feedback. It’s a powerful way to shape behavior, but deployment readiness depends on how well that whole process captures the situations the model will actually encounter.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not state that reinforcement learning consumes most post-training compute for large-scale models.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes reinforcement learning as “one part of post-training” and places it within the broader process of preparing a model for deployment.
